    17. Fubini’s theorem#

    Tonelli’s theorem (Theorem 16.1) exchanges the order of integration for every non-negative -measurable function on the product of two -finite measure spaces. Many integrands of interest change sign, such as or for integrable functions and . For such a function, the signed integral of Definition 8.11 is defined only when , as the difference of the integrals of the positive and negative parts. Tonelli’s theorem applies to and to separately, and subtracting the two identities yields the exchange of the order of integration for , provided no difference of the form appears. Fubini’s theorem states that integrability of with respect to suffices for this subtraction, both on and in the iterated integrals.

    The two theorems divide the work. Tonelli’s theorem, which needs no integrability, computes as an iterated integral and thereby verifies the hypothesis of Fubini’s theorem. Fubini’s theorem then exchanges the order of integration for itself. Its conclusions hold only almost everywhere: the inner integral is defined for the points at which the section is integrable, and these points form a set whose complement is -null.

    After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

    • State Fubini’s theorem with its hypotheses and its almost-everywhere conclusions, and compare it with Tonelli’s theorem.

    • Verify the integrability hypothesis of Fubini’s theorem by applying Tonelli’s theorem to .

    • Prove Fubini’s theorem from Tonelli’s theorem through the decomposition into positive and negative parts.

    • Explain, with an example, how the exchange of the order of integration fails for a function that is not integrable on the product, even when both iterated integrals are finite.

    • Apply Fubini’s theorem to products of integrable functions and to the exchange of series and integrals.

    Throughout these notes, and are -finite measure spaces and is their product measure on (Theorem 15.9). Sections are as in Definition 15.3. A measurable function is integrable if , and and are its positive and negative parts, so that and (Definition 8.10).

    A non-negative integrable function satisfies the hypotheses of both theorems; for such a function, Fubini’s theorem adds to Tonelli’s theorem only the information that the inner integrals are finite almost everywhere.

    The hypothesis (17.1) concerns the non-negative measurable function , so it is verified with Tonelli’s theorem.

    Remark 17.2 (Verifying the hypothesis of Fubini’s theorem)#

To exchange the order of integration for a signed function, we first compute or bound whichever iterated integral of is more convenient, and then apply Fubini’s theorem to . Computing the iterated integrals of itself does not verify the hypothesis: Section 17.3 exhibits a function whose two iterated integrals are finite and different.

    Tonelli’s and Fubini’s theorems together reduce integrals on product spaces to integrals in one variable: Tonelli’s theorem for non-negative integrands without any integrability hypothesis, and Fubini’s theorem for signed integrands once Tonelli’s theorem has shown that . Both theorems are the main tools for the convolution of functions on , which is defined by an integral over depending on a parameter.
